smm_pool.text: Meta advertisers are tired of turning off creative enhancements. I hear it all the time, and this cry has only become louder during the past year. It’s understandable. Say what you will about whether you need to turn enhancements off (I’ll get to that), but the number of Meta’s tweaks and adjustments that make your ad something that you or a client never approved is staggering. I’m covering 47 of them in this post, and I’m surely missing some. I do think most advertisers overreact to many of these enhancements, and they should probably just leave them on rather than fight it. Some can be customized to better fit their needs. But there absolutely are examples when many should be turned off, and it often depends on the situation. Some of these enhancements are well known to advertisers because they’re obvious steps in the ad creation flow. Others are buried settings that are easy to miss. We’re not going to miss them today. Let’s go through all 47 of the possible enhancements you may encounter, what they do, whether you can turn them off, and how I approach them. I’ll also finish with my general recommended approach to these enhancements. Settings: Extensions There are several settings that impact how various enhancements appear. These Extensions are found during the first step after uploading an image or video. 1. Website Summaries: Website Summaries are generated with AI based on information from your website and Instagram profile. These key words and phrases are highlighted under your ad. On/Off: You can turn off summaries by unchecking it or remove individual highlights by clicking on the ones you don’t want. I tend to leave this on. 2. Branding: This step is often missed, but it has a huge impact on enhancements. Provide your company logo, font, colors, and visual style to influence appearance. Use text tone and restricted words to impact AI-generated text. On/Off: This isn’t something that can be turned off, but you need to dedicate some time to defining your branding. 3. Site Links: Meta can identify important Site Links from your website that could be highlighted in various enhancements. If you don’t edit these, you’re putting an awful lot of trust in Meta’s automated systems. You can control the links that are featured, labels, and the icons used for them. smm_pool.title: How Long Should Instagram Reels Be? We Analyzed 2.7 Million Reels
smm_pool.text: You're here because you're wondering how long Instagram Reels can be. Have you thought about how long they should be? Creating a well-watched Instagram Reel is just as much art as it is science. I think folks will be surprised to hear the latter — but working with the Instagram algorithm requires some rigorous experimentation. Scroll-stopping hooks, post timing, keywords, and reel length are all variables I’ve held under the microscope on my Instagram creator journey . (Demystifying the black box that is a social media algorithm is my Roman Empire.) And now I have some quantitative data on Instagram Reel length. We looked at over 2.7 million Instagram Reels published through Buffer between January 1 and August 15, 2026, with the help of Buffer’s data science team (thank you, Steve and Iggy !). This study was fascinating! I almost expected the super-short clips to be the top performers, especially in terms of reach and engagement . That couldn’t have been further from the truth. Reels between 90 seconds and three minutes got the most reach . Reels longer than 3 minutes got the most engagement. 👉 Before the numbers, the usual terms and conditions apply. The effect is real but modest — we're talking about single-digit percentages. And this is an association, rather than a cheat code: stretching your next reel to 100 seconds will not add 7% to your reach by itself. If you're interested in the methodology behind the study, you'll find that below. First, we'll get straight into the Instagram limits. How to post a reel longer than three minutes Instagram Reels vs. TikTok vs. YouTube Shorts length Study methodology How long can Instagram Reels be? Instagram Reels can be up to 20 minutes long, whether you record in the Instagram camera or upload from your camera roll. (This rolled out gradually, so a few accounts may still see a 90-second or three-minute cap.) The catch is that only reels of three minutes or less are eligible for recommendation to new audiences. smm_pool.title: We’re running an A/B test on human and AI involvement in hiring
smm_pool.text: We’re hiring for two roles, and trying two very different experiments We’ve spent many hours debating when, where, and how AI should fit into our hiring process. As a small team with a lot of ambition, we are trying to level up, and hiring is ripe for this level of innovation. At the same time, we want to keep a high level of human touch and judgment in hiring. It’s such a key area, when each hire has a huge impact on our goals and culture. For a long time, our process rested on the idea that a Buffer teammate would carefully read every application. That came from a good place, and we’re proud of it. At today’s volume, though, it has meant long waits for candidates and stretched-thin hiring managers. We know we need to modernize our process so we can do better, both for the people applying to Buffer and for our hiring managers. On the flip side, if you’ve looked for a job lately, you know the market is tough right now. It can be incredibly competitive, and at times fairly inhuman. And, it’s been tough to be on the hiring side in its own way. More and more of the applications we see are largely written by AI. We understand why; applying to a job (or many) can be draining, and job seekers need to preserve their time and mental health. But that has made it harder for us to spot the thoughtful and personal applications, and get back to people in a reasonable amount of time. So, we’re testing two ways to get there. We’re opening two roles, with very different application processes, as an experiment. Our goal is to learn as much as we can about the pros and cons of each approach, as we work to build a thoughtful hiring process that’s both efficient and deeply caring in a post-AI world. Here’s how we’re running these experiments. Experiment 1: Engineering Manager: a much lighter way to raise your hand. For our EM role, we’re making it much easier to say “I’m interested.” A short intro instead of a long application. Our applications have always asked a lot: a series of detailed questions about the work and the person applying. We loved getting to know people that way, but it was a big investment for the candidate, and it stings when it doesn’t work out. This time, we’re just asking for your profile and a short introduction, so we can do more of the work to understand your experience before asking more of you. smm_pool.title: We are Retiring Start Page: Why and What to Expect
smm_pool.text: As Buffer has continued to support the individuals, creators, and small and medium businesses who use us, we've had to balance being a relatively small team with making tough decisions. We've had to make one of these recently. After careful deliberation as a team, we've decided to retire Start Page. If you've built a Start Page with us, thank you. Creators, small businesses, and nonprofits have used it as a front door to their work since 2021. Many of our customers were just getting started with their online journey, and a full website can be expensive and fiddly to maintain. Start Page provided a simple, flexible page anyone could build in minutes and share across their social profiles. We don't take ending that lightly, which is why we're giving several months' notice, firm dates, and multiple options to make the transition as hassle-free as possible Here's the timeline: November 4, 2026: We've stopped allowing the creation of new Start Pages November 30, 2026: You'll have tools to move your page somewhere else. February 2, 2027: We'll begin taking down Start Pages that haven't been migrated somewhere else. I'd like to elaborate on why we're doing this, the plan moving forward, and what options we plan to have available. Why we're doing this Having one link that holds everything (also referred to as a link-in-bio tool) is still useful in today's social space. So why are we moving away from it? For us at Buffer, three things have become hard to ignore. We've focused Buffer on our core strengths outside of Start Page. Buffer is a social media toolkit: we help you plan, publish, and learn from your content, and engage with your community across the social channels you use. While Start Page lives in your bio, it sits off to the side of all that. We've wanted to work on Start Page, but it takes away from Buffer's strengths and focus. From a capabilities perspective, Start Page has fallen behind, and catching up would cost us the things you rely on. Link-in-bio and microsite tools have come a long way since 2021, and Start Page hasn't kept pace. Making it best-in-class would mean pulling several teammates away from other key, much-requested improvements to other core Buffer features. We don't think that's the right trade for most of our customers. It's challenging to run well as a small, nimble team. But its $149/user per month starting price ($99 if you pay annually) puts it out of reach for many creators, entrepreneurs, and businesses. And with no free plan, there's no way to get Hootsuite for free beyond the 14-day trial. Hootsuite has to earn its place in the budget, especially when you're already juggling a stack of tools just to keep your content running. I’m a former social media manager and creator, and I’ve used more than my fair share of social media management and analytics platforms. In this article, we’ll explore several of the best Hootsuite competitors and alternatives, how much they cost, who they’re best suited for, and what their best features look like.
